name: flock
description: See every Claude Code session you're running as one live tree — who forked from whom, who's working, and who's waiting on you.

viewsWelcome.contents:
No live Claude Code sessions found.
[New Claude Session](command:lineage.newSession)
[New Project](command:lineage.newProject)
A project is a name and a directory; every session running in it groups under it. Add a second directory later and each one gets a row of its own.
Flock reads `claude agents --json` every few seconds. If sessions are running but none appear, set `lineage.claudeBinary` to the full path of your claude CLI.

No active Claude Code sessions. Closed ones are hidden by the session filter.
[Show Closed Sessions Too](command:lineage.showAllSessions)
[New Claude Session](command:lineage.newSession)

No AI accounts yet.
[Add Account](command:lineage.addAccount)
An account is one subscription you can launch sessions on — a work plan, a personal plan, an API key. Each gets its own config directory, so you sign in once per account and never again.

lineage.claudeBinary.description: Full path to the claude CLI. Empty = search PATH.

enumDescriptions: Use tmux when it is installed (never on Windows). Sessions Flock launches run inside a private tmux server, invisible — no status bar, no prefix key.
Never use tmux. Sessions run as bare claude processes; workspace switches park them by closing and resume them from their transcripts.
lineage.tmux.description: Run Flock-launched Claude sessions inside a private tmux server (`tmux -L lineage`). This upgrades workspace parking from close-and-resume to detach-and-reattach: switching away hides a session's tab while the conversation KEEPS RUNNING — busy ones too — and switching back reattaches it instantly, live state intact. Requires tmux on PATH; without it (and always on Windows) Flock falls back to close-and-resume. Sessions started outside Flock are never wrapped either way.

enumDescriptions: Open the session as a normal editor tab, alongside your files.
Open the session in the terminal panel at the bottom.
Open the session as an editor tab and immediately move it into its own window.
lineage.terminalLocation.description: Where a Claude session's terminal opens.

enumDescriptions: Flock opens the session itself, in a tmux-backed terminal it owns. Every verb applies.
Hand new conversations to the official Claude Code extension (claude-vscode.newConversation). Requires that extension; without it Flock falls back to opening the session itself.
lineage.launch.mode.markdownDescription:
Who opens a **new** conversation.

`flock` opens it here, in a terminal Flock owns. `claudeExtension` runs the official Claude Code extension's **New Conversation** command instead, and adopts the session onto a tree row once `claude agents --json` reports it.

In `claudeExtension` mode Flock does not own the process, so these stop working for sessions started that way: **tmux parking** (a workspace switch closes the session instead of hiding it), **Close** and **Close with Summary**, **account pinning and per-account routing**, the **wrap prompt**, and **Flock-named tabs**. The tree row, the fork edge, the age, the status dot, the bell, project membership, branch colours, **Fork** and **Copy Session ID** all keep working.

**Fork is never delegated.** No command the extension contributes accepts a session id, so a fork has nothing to hand over and always opens Flock's own terminal. Picking an account by hand (**New Session From…**) also overrides the mode, because a delegated launch carries the delegate's own environment and cannot be pinned.

lineage.groupByFolder.description: Group sessions that no project claims by their working directory.

lineage.onlyProjectSessions.description: Show only sessions that belong to one of your projects. The roster is machine-wide, so this is the fastest way to stop seeing every directory anyone ever ran claude in. Ignored while you have no projects.

lineage.onlyActiveSessions.description: Show only sessions that are still running. Closed, exited and inferred-ancestor rows are filtered out of the tree — nothing is deleted, and a live session forked from a closed one keeps its place. This is the "Show Only Active Sessions" toggle in the view title.

lineage.showGhosts.description: Show exited ancestor sessions that live sessions were forked from.

lineage.showArchived.description: Show ALL closed sessions found in ~/.claude/projects, even ones this tree never knew. Off by default: your own sessions already stay in the tree after their tab closes (as dimmed, resumable inactive rows, until you delete them) — this switch only adds foreign history on top.

lineage.showPhantomRows.description: Show roster rows that are not sessions: entries whose process has exited but that `claude agents --json` never reaped, and `claude bg-spare` daemon warm-spares (pre-forked processes waiting to be claimed, which report an inherited name and a frozen status). Off by default — these cannot be focused, forked or resumed, and a stuck spare will pin the attention badge on the view indefinitely. Turn on to debug the roster.

lineage.staleAfterHours.description: Age at which "Delete Stale Sessions..." pre-ticks a session. This never removes anything on its own — it only decides which checkboxes start ticked in that command.

lineage.busyStaleMinutes.description: How long a session may keep the CLI's "busy" status with an untouched transcript before Flock stops drawing the running (amber) dot and shows it as idle. `claude agents --json` sometimes freezes a session's status at `busy` after its turn actually ended (most often an interactive session you finished with); a genuinely working session writes its transcript within seconds, so silence this long means it is done. Raise it if a long single tool call briefly flips to idle; turn on "Show Phantom Rows" to see the raw, uncorrected status.

lineage.hooks.enabled.description: Read the Claude Code hook event stream for instant updates. "Install Instant-Update Hooks…" sets this for you — installing the plugin only makes Claude write the events, this is the switch that makes Flock read them. The plugin lives in a skills directory and never edits ~/.claude/settings.json.

lineage.notifications.enabled.description: Track finished sessions: a session that completes a turn while you are elsewhere gets a green dot (also on its project row) until you look at it, and appears under the bell in the sidebar title. Turn off to go back to the plain waiting-only dot. Per-session override: right-click a session → Mute / Unmute Notifications.

lineage.notifications.popup.description: Also show a toast with a Focus button when a session finishes a turn while you are not looking at it. Off by default — with many parallel sessions the bell and the dots carry the same information without the interruptions.

lineage.workspaces.enabled.description: Show the workspace switcher in the status bar. A workspace scopes this window to one project: switching saves the current tab layout under the project you leave, hides what does not belong to the target, and restores the target's saved layout. Foreign sessions are parked: with tmux installed (see `lineage.tmux`) their tab hides while the conversation keeps running — busy ones included — and reattaches when you switch back; without tmux the terminal closes and the conversation resumes from its transcript, in which case busy sessions are never closed. Unsaved editors and terminals Flock does not own are never touched. The terminal panel is never used. KNOWN ISSUE in 0.1.2: a switch decides membership by containment while the sidebar decides it by longest match, so if one project's directory contains another's the two disagree and both projects' saved layouts can name the same session. If your projects nest, leave workspace mode or turn this off.

lineage.workspaces.resumeSessions.description: When switching to a project workspace, resume its parked sessions from their transcripts (up to 8 per switch). Parking closes a session's terminal when you switch away, so with this OFF nothing is parked at all — foreign session tabs stay open instead.

lineage.workspaces.autoSwitch.description: Focus follows project: when you start working in a session that belongs to another project, the window switches to that project's workspace by itself — the layout you leave is saved, foreign tabs hide, the project's saved layout comes back. Nothing is stopped and nothing asks a question. Turn off to switch only via the status bar / command.

lineage.explorer.followProject.description: The Explorer follows the active project: switching projects swaps the built-in file tree to that project's directories — the main one on top, any extra connected directories as their own collapsible roots below it, wherever they live on disk. Outline and Timeline are untouched. Requires running "Flock: Follow the Active Project in the Explorer" once per window, which converts it to a Flock workspace (one reload, then switching is instant and no terminal is lost). With this off, an already-converted window keeps its folders where they are.

enumDescriptions: One root: the directory you are working in. Which one that is follows the session you have focused, so the file tree moves with you. The Project view lists the rest — click one to send the tree there.
Every connected directory as its own collapsible root, the main one on top. The shape Flock shipped before this setting existed.
lineage.explorer.scope.markdownDescription: How much of the active project the Explorer shows. `directory` keeps the file tree to the one directory you are in, the way a plain folder window does; `project` shows every connected directory as its own root. Only applies when `#lineage.explorer.followProject#` is on. Takes effect on the next project switch — no reload.

lineage.accounts.enabled.description: Show the Accounts view, where each AI subscription you can launch sessions on gets a row: which plan it is, how much of its five-hour and weekly windows is gone, and which one new sessions use by default. Each account keeps its own config directory, so signing in to one never signs you out of another, and a session stays on the account it started on for life — resuming or forking it re-uses that account whatever the routing says today. Turn off if you only ever use one account; nothing about how sessions launch changes, the view just stops taking up sidebar space. The section is also gated on lineage.accounts.section, which is on by default and is the switch to reach for if you would rather have Flock's buttons on the FLOCK row.

lineage.accounts.section.markdownDescription:
Draw **Accounts** as a second section of the Flock sidebar. On by default: the accounts are worth a row of their own.

The only reason to turn it off is the top bar. VS Code merges a view's buttons into the container header — the row that reads **FLOCK** — only while that container shows exactly one section, so while Accounts is drawn the bell, New Project, `+`, fork and the gear sit on the **SESSIONS** row just below it instead. Off moves them up one row, and costs you the Accounts section.

Nothing about accounts stops working while it is off. Usage is still read, new sessions are still routed, a session is still pinned to its account for life, and every account verb — **Add Account…**, **Sign In**, **Set Default Account**, **Set Project Account…** — is in the Command Palette under **Flock**. The switch is also in the gear menu at the top of the sidebar.

enumDescriptions: Rename a session in place on its row, the way the Explorer renames a file. The sidebar is drawn by the extension.
Use the built-in VS Code tree. Rename opens a box at the top of the window, because the tree API has no editable row.
lineage.viewStyle.markdownDescription: How the Sessions view is drawn. `inline` renames on the row like the Explorer; `native` uses the built-in tree widget. Takes effect on the next window reload.

lineage.showTokens.markdownDescription: Show how many tokens a session is carrying, left of the time-since-active. The number is the context the last assistant turn ran with (prompt + cache + output), read from the transcript — so it matches what `/context` reports and grows as the conversation does. Off by default: it is a second number on every row.

lineage.groupSessionsByBranch.markdownDescription: Nest a project's sessions under the git branch they are running on, instead of listing the branches and then the sessions. Each branch row becomes a container you can fold shut, with a `+` that starts a session in that worktree. Only applies to a project with two or more worktrees; a session that no shown branch accounts for stays directly under the project. Off by default.

lineage.branchColors.markdownDescription: Read only by `#lineage.git.branchDisplay#`'s `color` mode; `inline` tints nothing. Colours for the branch chips, in order — index 0 is the first branch under a project (usually `main`). Each entry is either a hex colour (`#7aa2f7`) or a VS Code theme colour id (`charts.blue`, `terminal.ansiCyan`). A short list fills the rest from the built-in muted palette; anything that is not one of those two shapes is ignored. Empty = the built-in palette, which softens the theme's own `charts.*` colours toward the editor foreground.

lineage.git.pullRequests.markdownDescription: **The one thing in Flock that reaches the network.** With this on, Flock runs `gh pr list --state all --limit 100 --json ...` in each project's repository and shows the pull request on each branch row — number, state and check rollup as a small chip, with **Open Pull Request in Browser** on the row's menu. It shells out to the [`gh` CLI](https://cli.github.com) you installed and authenticated: Flock makes no HTTP requests of its own, bundles no API client and never sees a token. Polled only while the Sessions view is visible, at most once every five minutes per repository, and cached. If `gh` is missing, not signed in, or the repository has no GitHub remote, the rows render exactly as they do with this off and one line goes to the **Flock** output channel. Off by default, because everything else in Flock is local.

lineage.git.branches.markdownDescription:
Show a project’s **git branches** as rows, with the worktree verbs (*New Worktree*, *Remove Worktree*), the per-branch colours and the pull-request chip.

Off by default. The feature works, but it is a lot of rows in a sidebar that has to stay readable — turn it on if you run one agent per worktree.

This does not change which project a session belongs to: a session in a linked checkout stays under the project that owns the repository either way.

enumDescriptions: The branch is written under the session — ⎇ feat/search-ranking ↑4 * — and the name goes back to the theme's colour. Says which checkout, and carries the state tokens on the row. Costs a row's height.

The session's name takes its branch's colour, and the project's branch rows are the key to it. Costs no width; says which sessions share a checkout, never which checkout. Ahead/behind, dirt and the pull request are in the hover.
lineage.git.branchDisplay.markdownDescription:
**How a session says which worktree it is running in.** Two ways of answering one question, both complete — the branch rows, the worktree verbs and the pull-request lookup are the same either way. Needs `#lineage.git.branches#` on; with that off there is nothing to display.

**`inline` is the default.** The branch is written under the session, the way a git prompt or the SCM view says it — `⎇ feat/search-ranking ↑4 *` — and the name keeps the theme's own colour. It answers *which* checkout, and carries the state tokens where they can be read without hovering. It costs **height**: twelve sessions become twenty-four rows' worth. Because nothing needs decoding, the branch rows are **shut by default** here and reached from a project's right-click — see **Show Branches**.

`color` is what Flock shipped, and it is denser. The session's name is tinted from a per-branch palette (`#lineage.branchColors#`) and the project's branch rows are the legend, so they are **open by default**. It costs no width at all and answers *are these two on the same thing* down a whole column at a glance. What it cannot say is *which* thing, and everything a colour cannot carry — `↑4 ↓3 *`, the request — moves into the hover.

A line is drawn only where it says something new: on a session whose worktree differs from the one above it, in a project with more than one checkout. A fork made in its parent's worktree gets none. See `#lineage.git.sessionBranchDetail#` for how much it says.

enumDescriptions: The branch name and where the checkout stands: ↑4 ahead, ↓3 behind, * uncommitted. Local files only.
Also the pull request (#128 ✓), `merged` on a branch whose request landed, and `local` on one that was never pushed.
lineage.git.sessionBranchDetail.markdownDescription:
How much the line under a session says, in `inline` mode — see `#lineage.git.branchDisplay#`. Colour mode has no line, so this does nothing there.

`standard` is the vocabulary git prompts and the SCM view already use — `↑4 ↓3 *` and nothing else — so it reads without anybody learning it, and it touches nothing but local files.

`detailed` adds the pull-request chip and the two states arrows render as blank: **`local`** for a branch that tracks nothing, and the word **`merged`**, which is the signal that the worktree can be removed. The chip half needs `#lineage.git.pullRequests#` on as well, since that is what fills the cache it reads.

lineage.git.worktreePath.markdownDescription: Where **New Worktree…** puts a new checkout. `${repo}` is the repository directory's name and `${branch}` the branch name with anything a path cannot carry replaced by `-`. A relative pattern is resolved against the repository's main worktree, so the default puts `feat/x` of `~/code/app` at `~/code/app-feat-x`. An absolute path is used as written, and a leading `~/` expands. Must contain `${branch}`, or every branch would resolve to the same directory. Flock always shows the exact `git worktree add` command before running it.

lineage.git.newSessionInWorktree.markdownDescription:
Make the **`+` on a project or subproject row** cut a **new worktree** first and start the session there, instead of starting it in the directory as it is.

One agent per checkout is the reason most people turn the branch feature on at all, and with this off that workflow costs a right-click every time. It changes the **button's default and nothing else**: both verbs — **New Session** and **New Session in New Worktree…** — are on the row's right-click whichever way this points, and the row's `+` says in its tooltip which one it is about to run.

The worktree half still confirms and still quotes the exact `git worktree add` before running it, and it uses `#lineage.git.worktreePath#` to decide where. Needs `#lineage.git.branches#` on.

lineage.preview.directoryModel.markdownDescription:
PREVIEW. Hang the branch rows off a **directory** instead of off the project, and list **every local branch** of that directory’s repository rather than only the checked-out ones.

A project’s directories are its subprojects, and a directory is exactly one git repository (or none) — so the directory is the row a branch belongs under. A project spanning three repositories no longer shows three branches called `main` with no way to tell which is which.

Outside the fold: the directory’s **own checkout**, and any branch with a **session running on it**. Everything else — including a worktree with nothing running in it — goes in one **Branches (N)** row, newest commit first, **shut by default**. That is what makes listing a 180-branch repository cost one row.

Needs `#lineage.git.branches#`. Draws in the inline sidebar (`#lineage.viewStyle#`: `inline`, the default); the native tree keeps the rows it has today.

lineage.preview.demoProject.markdownDescription:
PREVIEW. Add a **fabricated project** to the tree — *Flock (demo)* — to look at the directory-and-branch layout without needing a repository shaped the right way.

Three directories: one repository with two checkouts, one directory *inside* that repository, and one that is not a repository at all. Nothing on it is real, nothing on it can be clicked into existence, and it has **no sessions** — a session row comes from the real roster, so a made-up one would draw nothing. For sessions under a branch, use `#lineage.preview.directoryModel#` on your own projects.

Turning this off removes it completely.

walkthroughs.title: Get started with Flock
walkthroughs.description: Three things worth knowing before you run six agents at once.

steps.title: Your sessions are already here
steps.description:
Flock reads the Claude Code CLI's own session registry, so anything you have run `claude` on shows up with no setup.
[Open the Sessions view](command:workbench.view.extension.lineage)

steps.title: Start one from the tree
steps.description:
Press + on any project row. The session appears immediately with its name selected — type over it or press Enter. No dialog.
[New Claude Session](command:lineage.newSession)

steps.title: Watch the right edge
steps.description: Amber means working. Red means finished and not yet seen — like an unread message, it clears when you look. Everything else stays blank on purpose.
